title: Fold the shell tokenizer's delimiter-depth loops into one helper, and move the TypeScript span scanner into its own kernel module
text: Two behaviour-preserving refactors of the hermetic policy kernel under packages/lup/src/lup/policy/kernel/, each its own branch and commit. (1) kernel/syntax.py has four loops that walk a string counting delimiter depth: balanced_end (parentheses, depth 1, skips quoted strings and backslash escapes), brace_end (braces, depth 1, skips $( … ) via balanced_end), and the two arithmetic readers near lines 755-830 (parentheses, depth 2, one refusing backticks and $( inside). They differ only in delimiter pair, starting depth, and what they skip; one helper taking the pair and the skip rule replaces all four. (2) kernel/edit.py is 4000 lines and holds the TypeScript span scanner inside masked_typescript_lines: the nested literal_end, regex_end and template_piece readers and the character walk around them, roughly lines 700-830. The net: the tokenizer tests under packages/lup/tests/unit and tests/unit that import kernel.syntax, and test_antipatterns.py, which imports masked_typescript_lines directly. title: Native SendMessage as the wake for an idle Claude peer: why it never carries today, and what would make it
text: The coordination design says a Claude peer is woken through the native message tool: wake() in lup.coordination.wake returns, for a member with a claude handle, an instruction naming the caller's own SendMessage tool and the address to use, and docs/platform-differentiation.md (row Waking an idle peer) says the handle is self-reported on the roster because on Claude it can only be, since CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID and CLAUDE_CODE_BRIDGE_SESSION_ID are set and neither is what peers address a session by, which ListAgents reports. Observed on 2026-09-19: a handoff to a freshly opened session (dev-5, id cd6f3c588bb7) was recorded and mailed at 14:50 and the session never looked; coordination_send reported that the member declared no wake path. Three things stand between the design and a wake, and the investigation is to settle each and say what to build. First, nothing reports the handle: coordination join has no option for it, no roster record in the store's whole history carries one, and so the claude arm of wake() is dead code. Second, the native listing may not cross containment: this session runs contained (LUP_CONTAINED=1, its own CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET), and its ListAgents call returns no reachable session while the repository roster shows five running, so even a reported handle may name a session the tool cannot reach from here. Third, the peer policy landed on 2026-09-09 (commit 12408ff96, lup.policy.kernel.peers) denies a native send whose input names a live roster member, naming coordination_send as the durable surface; whether that denial would refuse the very send wake() instructs depends on whether the self-reported handle and the roster address are the same string, and the escalate hint on the denial may be the intended way through. Deliverable: which of the three actually stops the wake, in what order, with a measurement for each; then a proposal for the join-time handle report, the containment crossing, and the policy carve-out, as decisions for the user.
open_questions: How a session learns its own native handle at join time. ListAgents prints it for the session itself (this one reads as antipattern-match-case [36024e]), but the SessionStart hook that joins the roster runs before any tool call; check whether the handle is derivable from the environment or the messaging socket, or whether the first prompt hook has to report it after the fact

Whether native messaging crosses containment. Measure from two sessions: one contained, one on the host, each calling ListAgents; and read what CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET points at inside a container versus on the host. If sockets are container-local, decide between mounting the host socket into contained launches and relaying through a host-side session that holds the tool

Whether decide_peer_send in lup.policy.kernel.peers would deny the send that wake() instructs. It matches every string the call carries against the roster's live addresses, whole values only; settle whether a self-reported handle would ever equal a roster address, and whether the denial needs a carve-out for a send that carries mail already recorded, or whether the escalate hint is the intended route

Whether the delivery hook should keep the wake even once one exists: the inbox mode already fronts a working session's next call, so the wake matters only for an idle session, and the docs should say which of the two a sender is getting

title: Native SendMessage as the wake for an idle Claude peer: why it never carries today, and what would make it
text: All three stop the wake, and they stop it in this order: nothing reports a handle, so wake() never emits the instruction; the peer policy denies the send the instruction names; and past the policy the runtime cannot resolve the peer at all. The third is decisive — it is the only one that still stops the send when the other two are lifted, measured by escalating past the policy and watching the send return 'No agent named dev-5 is reachable' while six sessions were live on the roster. The cause is that native peer discovery is a scan of a socket directory on the local filesystem, and under containment that directory is the container's own overlay holding exactly one socket. Two premises the investigation started from are wrong. The handle is not something only a session can self-report: the launcher passes `--name member.cli_name` to claude and exports the same string as LUP_COORDINATION_NAME, so join time already knows it, and docs/platform-differentiation.md's 'on Claude it can only be' holds for an unlaunched session only. And because the launcher makes the two names one string, the policy denial is structural rather than a coincidence of spelling — every wake a launched session instructs names a live roster address. What is left is three decisions, which are the user's: whether to cross containment at all and how, whether to declare the handle at join, and what shape the policy carve-out takes. Nothing was changed; the session holds nothing.
open_questions: DECISION (user): whether to cross containment at all, and how. Claude Code offers `--remote-control [name]`, whose sessions ListAgents says it lists across machines — that crosses containers because it routes through the account rather than the filesystem, and it sends session traffic off the machine. A shared socket directory bind-mounted into every contained launch is the local alternative and needs the pid-7 socket-name collision and the per-namespace peer verification solved first. Doing nothing is a real third answer: the wake would still work between two host-posture sessions, and contained sessions would keep the durable inbox they have

DECISION (user): whether to declare the handle at join, and from where. It needs no new self-reporting surface — RepositoryPeers.join() already holds cli_name, which is the string the launcher gave claude as --name, so it can pass WakePath(runtime='claude', handle=cli_name) today. The open part is what happens after a native /rename, which moves the display name and not the roster name, leaving a declared handle stale; the alternative is having the session read its own name off ListAgents on its first tool call and report it then

DECISION (user): what shape the policy carve-out takes. The escalate line works but asks a reviewer on every wake, which is wrong for an automatic nudge. The carve-out that can be checked rather than trusted is the store's own record: decide_peer_send already receives the store directory, so it can allow a native send to a member that has mail from this sender it has not yet read — which is exactly 'a wake on top of the record' and still denies the record-losing send the rule exists for

Whether the delivery hook should keep the wake even once one exists: the inbox mode already fronts a working session's next call, so the wake matters only for an idle session, and the docs should say which of the two a sender is getting

Whether two host-posture sessions can in fact wake each other, which is the one claim here that is inferred rather than measured: it rests on the binary's socket-directory patterns plus /tmp/cc-socks being an ordinary host directory. One `ls -la /tmp/cc-socks/` from a host terminal with two host sessions running settles it

title: Native SendMessage as the wake for an idle Claude peer: why it never carries today, and what would make it
text: Containment is the cause, and the wake mechanism is intact — both demonstrated rather than argued. Two Claude sessions inside one container, sharing one /tmp/cc-socks, discover each other (ListAgents listed the second as 'longprobe [88d4e9] · interactive · busy'), a native SendMessage to it returned success, and the peer dropped its own work and answered the message. The five peers on this repository's roster are unreachable for exactly one reason: each runs in its own container, where /tmp is the container's own overlay, so each session's socket directory holds only its own socket. Nothing about wake() or the runtime broke; visibility did, when contained launches became the posture on 2026-08-25 (fa3cc672b, hardened ae7ccdad7 and c35a99051). Two earlier conclusions in this record were wrong and are corrected below: the policy stop is not structural, and a same-container probe that saw nobody was blind in one direction only. What is left is three decisions, which are the user's: whether to declare a host bridge for the socket directory and how, whether to declare the handle at join, and what shape the policy carve-out takes.
open_questions: DECISION (user): whether to declare a host bridge for the socket directory, the way ClipboardBridge, /run/lup/browser and the /run/lup/ssh-agent bind already cross the wall. The mechanism is now demonstrated, so this is a question of whether to open the channel rather than whether it would work. Two things to settle first: whether CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET is an input, which decides the pid-7 socket-name collision; and whether peer verification survives a pid-namespace crossing, since verifiedPeerProcStart and ownerUids resolve pid 7 to the reader's own claude. --remote-control is the non-local alternative and needs no bridge, at the cost of sending session traffic off the machine

DECISION (user): whether to declare the handle at join, and from where. It needs no new self-reporting surface — RepositoryPeers.join() already holds cli_name, which is the string given to --name, measured. The open part is what happens after a native /rename, which moves the display name and not the roster name, leaving a declared handle stale; the alternative is having the session read its own name off ListAgents on its first tool call and report it then

DECISION (user): what shape the policy carve-out takes, now that the stop is known to be inconsistent rather than structural — it denies a wake to a session still carrying its launch name and permits one to a session that renamed. The carve-out that can be checked rather than trusted is the store's own record: decide_peer_send already receives the store directory, so it can allow a native send to a member holding unread mail from this sender, which is exactly 'a wake on top of the record'

Whether a genuinely IDLE peer wakes, as against the busy one demonstrated here. The peer that answered 'woken at 3000' was mid-turn; the vendor contract says a message drains at the receiver's next tool round and ListAgents labels a peer idle or busy, but the idle case was not separately measured because a -p session is never idle. It wants one lingering interactive session

Whether the delivery hook should keep the wake even once one exists: the inbox mode already fronts a working session's next call, so the wake matters only for an idle session, and the docs should say which of the two a sender is getting

title: Native SendMessage as the wake for an idle Claude peer: why it never carries today, and what would make it
text:
SETTLED by the user: keep SendMessage as the wake channel. The full write-up is tmp/peer-wake-briefing.md, rewritten whole and graded measured/read/open; this node is the durable index and the briefing is what a fresh session reads.

The decisive measurement, which should have been taken first and was taken last: a native SendMessage DOES wake an idle session. A background session confirmed idle by the harness's own idle notice and by ListAgents was sent a token and its logs show it taking a turn and answering it. Everything else rests on that.

All three original blockers fire, in the order handle -> policy -> containment, and containment is decisive: escalated past the policy the send returned 'No agent named dev-5 is reachable' while six sessions were live. Peer discovery is a scan of a socket directory that containment makes container-local; a shared directory fixes it, and the two things that would have sunk that are measured and neither does (the runtime disambiguates colliding socket names itself; peer verification survives a pid-namespace crossing).

Four alternative shapes were explored and rejected, and the briefing records why so nobody re-derives them: recording the native send and permitting it (rejected by the user -- the record survives but the habit that carries work to peers which do not exist yet does not); a host-side tmux send-keys nudge (rejected by the user; mechanically sound, and the tmux server is on the host and deliberately unbridged); lup holding the terminal itself (it wires an operator's session -it and hands the terminal through, so it would have to write a multiplexer); and the receiver arming a watch on its own inbox (viable, needs no bridge at all, but something must arm it and a hook cannot).

Landed: fix-launcher-env-hermeticity, on dev at cb608dd03 -- the incidental find, and the widest. Committed and unlanded: feat-messaging-bridge and feat-wake-handle, both gated green. Abandoned: feat-recorded-peer-send, whose worktree still holds the uncommitted half-build of the rejected shape.
open_questions: DECISION (user): confirm the fixed content-free nudge as the carve-out, and what the nudge says. A send to a roster member is permitted only where its text is exactly one declared string, so the channel can only ever carry 'go look'; every other text stays denied, which keeps the diagnostic that teaches coordination_send and leaves one habit for sending content. Its costs are one extra call for the woken peer, and brittleness -- an agent that paraphrases is denied, so the deny text and wake()'s instruction must both carry the exact string

DECISION (user): whether `codex queue` gets the same rule in the same change. `dev policy 'codex queue --thread x --message y'` answers that the command is not classified, so the peer policy is Claude-only in effect and a Codex agent can reach a peer from a shell with no record at all. That hole exists today, independently of this work

DECISION (user): whether feat-messaging-bridge is load-bearing or convenience. Under the chosen design it is load-bearing, since without it the wake reaches nobody -- worth confirming because it also widens what agents can do: unlike the browser and clipboard bridges, which cross between a session and its operator, it crosses between two sessions
DECISION (user): landing order for the two ready branches, against dev-2's stack and the new stage-then-fast-forward route in /lup:land

Whether `codex queue` wakes an idle Codex session or only queues for its next turn, and whether the Codex app-server daemon socket crosses containment. Both need a signed-in Codex session and its standalone install; this machine has the npm install and no credentials, measured with codex doctor. The Codex levers are documented and better than Claude's -- `app-server proxy --sock` takes the socket path as an input, `queue`/`agents` take `--remote unix://PATH`, and $CODEX_HOME/app-server-daemon follows CODEX_HOME, verified by relocating it

Whether a nudge to a busy peer is noisy in practice. The library cannot tell busy from idle -- ListAgents can, but only a session may call it -- so a nudge fires on every send to a handle-declaring peer

WHAT IS MEASURED NOW. Every Claude session runs a private UDS inbox, and the binary documents the injection protocol itself: newline-delimited {"type":"auth","token":...} then {"type":"user","message":{...}}. Injection works with NO auth frame at all -- no token is needed, only reachability of the socket. An idle background session was woken this way by a plain Python script and answered. --messaging-socket-path relocates a session's inbox (the env var does not), and a session woken through a relocated socket answered. So wake() on Claude can finish the job itself exactly as codex queue does on Codex: the Claude/Codex asymmetry this node recorded DOES NOT EXIST, and no policy carve-out for a native SendMessage is needed.

Discovery is two paths, not one: a socket-directory scan (container-local under containment) plus a registry at $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/sessions/ carrying messagingSocketPath, name and status -- which only kind:"bg" sessions publish to, which is why ListAgents shows nobody while interactive peers are live. The earlier 'do not redo' entries saying there is no second discovery path in /cfg, and that nothing relocates a session's socket, are both wrong.

DESIGN SETTLED WITH THE USER: shape gamma -- lup passes --messaging-socket-path for every session it launches, and wake() injects directly, falling back to the runtime's default scan paths for a hand-launched session carrying the plugin. title: Three steps only the operator can take: two upstream reports, #494, and the tracker credential
text:
The Codex subagent-parity work is implemented and on dev. What is left cannot be done from a session.

1. **The tracker credential is dead.** `gh auth status` says the token in GH_TOKEN is invalid since the rotation, so nothing here reads or writes the tracker. `dev issues` now says so and exits 1 rather than printing "0 open issue(s)".

2. **Close #494** once the credential is back. The verdict is settled and durable without it: both halves of the Codex subagent leak were measured and they come apart — work a subagent arms outlives its report, and output forced onto it resumes nobody. So the Codex tree registers `SubagentStart` alone, with its own host half, and deliberately registers no stop-time refusal. Row 65 of docs/platform-differentiation.md states both measurements; `lup.providers.codex.assets.subagent_cleanup` carries the same in its docstring.

3. **File the two upstream reports**, whose `gh issue create` lines are printed in docs/upstream-reports.md. `subagent-session-outlives-thread` goes to openai/codex and wants the two subagent rollouts attached — they sit at the `agent_transcript_path` each `SubagentStop` carried, in the operator's home, unreadable from a session. `list-agents-ref-collision` goes to anthropics/claude-code and needs nothing attached. Both stay "not filed" in the declaration until somebody records the URL there.

The probe kits stay on disk until the Codex report is filed: tmp/codex-subagent-probe (31 records, two runs) and tmp/codex-rewake-probe (20 records).
open_questions: Whether the leaked PTY warrants anything beyond the start-time sentence: the sentence is registered, and nothing has yet measured whether a Codex subagent acts on it.
not_again: Re-measuring whether Codex resumes a finished subagent: it does not, measured twice on 0.155.1 with every event registered, and the negative is read off the hook record rather than from the run's own answer.
Porting Claude Code's SubagentStop block to Codex: it would refuse a report to prevent a loop that runtime does not have.
Reading the tracker from a session until the credential is replaced: every call answers HTTP 401.

WHAT IS MEASURED NOW. Every Claude session runs a private UDS inbox, and the binary documents the injection protocol itself: newline-delimited {"type":"auth","token":...} then {"type":"user","message":{...}}. Injection works with NO auth frame at all -- no token is needed, only reachability of the socket. An idle background session was woken this way by a plain Python script and answered. --messaging-socket-path relocates a session's inbox (the env var does not), and a session woken through a relocated socket answered. So wake() on Claude can finish the job itself exactly as codex queue does on Codex: the Claude/Codex asymmetry this node recorded DOES NOT EXIST, and no policy carve-out for a native SendMessage is needed.

Discovery is two paths, not one: a socket-directory scan (container-local under containment) plus a registry at $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/sessions/ carrying messagingSocketPath, name and status -- which only kind:"bg" sessions publish to, which is why ListAgents shows nobody while interactive peers are live. The earlier 'do not redo' entries saying there is no second discovery path in /cfg, and that nothing relocates a session's socket, are both wrong.

DESIGN SETTLED WITH THE USER: shape gamma -- lup passes --messaging-socket-path for every session it launches, and wake() injects directly, falling back to the runtime's default scan paths for a hand-launched session carrying the plugin. The agent never touches the channel: the SendMessage deny stays absolute and coordination_send remains the one habit.

REJECTED BY THE USER, with reasons, so nobody re-derives them: alpha, the receiver's own MCP server injecting into its own session (verified workable -- the coordination server is a long-lived child holding its session's socket and token -- but it makes waking a property of the receiver's configuration, wrong for a framework running in other people's repositories); beta-full, sharing the runtime's default socket directory (more general, reaches any session on the machine, but creates machine-wide session-to-session reachability through a FILE channel that lup.policy.kernel.peers cannot see, and switches on the native unrecorded cross-container channel the policy exists to deny). Also rejected earlier and still rejected: recording the native send and permitting it; tmux send-keys; lup holding the terminal; the receiver arming its own watch.

BRANCHES. Landed: fix-launcher-env-hermeticity (cb608dd03). Keep and repurpose: feat-wake-handle (the identity seam keeps the Windows named-pipe case out of the library). Repurpose, do not land as built: feat-messaging-bridge (its shared-directory machinery is what gamma needs, retargeted off the runtime's path). Discard: feat-recorded-peer-send. Both live branches are 35 commits behind dev and their green gate was earned on that old base.

BUILD ORDER: fix-wake-via-uds (inject on Claude, correct wake.py and platform-differentiation row 68, re-pin the 18 verbs); feat-wake-handle merged up; feat-socket-placement (the launcher flag and shared directory); fix-peer-send-rename (close the roster-rename hole -- decide_peer_send matches the target NAME STRING so a natively renamed session receives anything -- and classify codex queue, which dev policy returns as ALLOWED when sandboxed). That last one matters most for an uncontained adopter, where the policy is the only bound there is.
open_questions: Whether `codex queue` wakes an idle Codex session or only queues for its next turn, and whether the Codex app-server daemon socket crosses containment. Both need a signed-in Codex session and its standalone install; this machine has the npm install and no credentials, measured with codex doctor. The Codex levers are documented and better than Claude's -- `app-server proxy --sock` takes the socket path as an input, `queue`/`agents` take `--remote unix://PATH`, and $CODEX_HOME/app-server-daemon follows CODEX_HOME, verified by relocating it

Whether a nudge to a busy peer is noisy in practice. The library cannot tell busy from idle -- ListAgents can, but only a session may call it -- so a nudge fires on every send to a handle-declaring peer
